## The Visual Bible

Work from the plan lines: an element a plan line only implies still needs an entry, because a page can reference only what is listed.

- All locations, all objects, all vehicles, all animals.
- A worn garment gets its own entry only when the story changes it: taken off, handed to another character, found, or worn by someone whose outfit does not name it. A garment that simply stays part of its owner's outfit gets no entry; the outfit text carries it.
- Secondary characters you invented only. Never Sarah, Saira, Facundo, Fiona, Lorena — they have reference photos.
- Every secondary-character entry carries `age` as a NUMBER of years (`8`, `34`), never prose, and opens `build` with the character's sex and body type ("a boy, slim", "a woman, broad-shouldered"), never a height or a size word — `scaleClass` carries the size. Jaw and facial-hair notes carry neither.

- An entry shaped like a person — an invented figure, a small winged being, a doll, a figurine, a statue, a puppet — states its HAIR in `description`: colour, length and how it is worn, or plainly that it has none. Such an entry reaches the image model as its description and nothing else, and a head described only by its eyes is drawn bald. State the head the same way a face is stated: hair, then whatever else the figure's head carries.
- Every named or story-significant vehicle, vessel or structure gets its own `vehicles` entry (ids VEH001…) — the antagonist's and the rival's included, never folded into `locations`. When two of them can share one frame, both need entries. A toy figure the story names or turns on (a teddy, a doll, a puppet, a plush animal) is an `artifacts` entry, with a `properName` when the story names it — never a secondary character (that is a person) and never an `animals` entry.
- Every Visual Bible element carries `scaleClass`, and it is the only place an element’s size is stated: [the element's scale band, one of: fingertip-sized, palm-sized, hand-sized, melon-sized, forearm-sized, arm-sized, knee-high, waist-high, chest-high, adult-height, twice-adult-height, house-height, landmark. Two questions, two groups — answer one of them, never both. HOW BIG IS IT, for a thing someone could pick up and hold; these bands say nothing about how tall it stands: fingertip-sized — a pea, a ring; palm-sized — an apple, a mouse; hand-sized — a book, a loaf; melon-sized — a football, a lantern, a helmet; forearm-sized — a rolling pin, a small cat; arm-sized — a broom, a shovel. HOW TALL DOES IT STAND, for a thing that rests on the ground and has a height; these bands say nothing about how bulky it is: knee-high — a dog, a stool; waist-high — a young child, a barrel; chest-high — a counter, a pony; adult-height — a doorway, a grown-up standing; twice-adult-height — a market stall with its roof; house-height — a house, a full-grown tree; landmark — a cliff, a mountain, the horizon behind everything. A band never carries the other group's meaning: a head-sized thing is melon-sized, never adult-height. Judge the element's largest dimension, not how the story feels about it. The story states a size only where its plot turns on one, so the band is yours to decide from what the story has the element do — held in one hand, lifted by two, ridden, hidden under a bed. This is the only place the element's size is stated. Never omitted.] An adjective is not a band — massive, tiny, huge name none. No entry gives a size of its own, in words or in units.
- `generic: true` only when any instance of the thing would serve: swap it between two pages and no reader could tell. If the story ever refers back to THIS one — it is found, lost, given, marked, recognised, or a character owns it — it is not generic. A generic element gets no entry beyond that flag, no id and no reference image: it is named in the page's scene prose like any other physical fact and never appears in `objects[]`. Omit the field on every other element.
- Lettering the reader must actually READ — a signpost a character reads, a labelled door, a numbered house, a name on a gift — is declared: the element carrying it gets an entry whose `text` is the exact characters in the order they must appear. Nothing else declares `text`: writing the story never asks anyone to read stays undeclared and its `description` calls it illegible. A page whose prose has someone read something cites an entry that declares the string, and an entry is written for it when none exists. Many instances of one lettered thing — a row of marked posts, a shelf of labelled jars — are ONE entry with a plural label whose `text` is the whole run in the order it must read across them, and such an entry is never `generic`.
- A name the story gives an element lives in `properName` and nowhere else — never in `label`, `name`, `description` or the page prose. One `properName` belongs to one id: two entries never share a name. An object that transforms later in the story and the creature it becomes are separate ids, and only one of them carries the name.
- `label` is the one English name every prompt uses for an element: one to four words ending in the noun, unique in this bible, never a bare category, never a proper noun, never a word from the story language.
- English `name` and `description` for artifacts, locations, vehicles and clothing, even for a non-English story; those strings are copied into English image prompts. Characters and animals keep their given names.
- Every item in exactly one category. A worn garment belongs to `clothing` only, never also to `artifacts`. Exception: a prop the story turns into costume (a hat found in a chest, a cloak handed over) is ONE `artifacts` entry with `wornAs`: `"<CharacterName>.<slot>"`. Every garment a listed character wears is one their outfits in AVAILABLE CLOTHING PER CHARACTER name, and its entry's `description` repeats the outfit's words for it. Never dress a listed character in a garment their outfits do not name, and never reword one; a page without a garment says so in a `wornItems` row. The slot is one of `headwear`, `top`, `bottom`, `footwear`, `belt/waist`, `outer layer`, `accessories` and never another word; neckwear, handwear and eyewear are `accessories`. `wornAs` is REQUIRED on any entry whose `type` is an outfit slot or whose item an outfit above also describes; without it no page can say who wears it. `wornAs` names where the item lives and never changes — which character wears it on a given page is that page's `wornItems` row.
- Every worn garment's entry — each `clothing` entry and each entry with `wornAs` — carries `back`: the garment as seen from behind, one short phrase of its colour, material and outline, plus anything that sits on its back (a hood, a back print). Nothing only its front shows: no front fastening, front pockets, collar opening, buttons or front print.
- Every entry a character wears on the body — each `clothing` entry, and each `artifacts` entry that is part of an outfit — carries `slot`: where on the body it is worn, exactly one of `headwear`, `top`, `bottom`, `footwear`, `belt/waist`, `outer layer`, `accessories`, and never another word; neckwear, handwear, eyewear and a bag or backpack worn on the body are `accessories`. When the entry also has `wornAs`, `slot` is the slot named there. Anything not worn on the body has no `slot` field at all, whatever its name says: an object that is held, carried in the hand, hung up, tied round another object, set on a pole or lying somewhere.
- An animal's `features` are its anatomy on every page — eye colour and shape, markings, horns, snout, the mouth and its teeth ("a closed, rounded mouth", "a soft rounded snout"), collar — each stated as something the animal has, never as an absence. Never an expression, an emotion, a smile or a mood word (friendly, gentle, calm, kind, happy, relaxed): a face's feeling changes page by page and each page brief writes it.
- A change to an object, an animal or an invented figure is a state, not a second entry. One physical thing is ONE entry however the story alters it — broken, mended, opened, filled; a wing broken then whole; a coat lost then found. Almost every entry has no states at all: the field exists for the rare thing the story itself changes, and an entry without one is the normal case. `description` holds how it is BUILT — the material, shape and size that survive every state. `states[]` lists every look it wears, each with its own `pages`, because each state is drawn as its own reference cell and there is no separate cell for the object at rest. The FIRST state is therefore not optional and not implied by `description`: it is the object before the story changes anything, and it carries every page up to the first change. Leave it out and those pages are drawn in the first CHANGE instead — an object already broken, muddied or emptied on the page it is found. Two entries for one object give it two canonical descriptions and two reference renders that disagree on how it is built.
- The bible shows the OBJECT and nothing else. The test for a state: take away everything that is not the object — the hands, the hole, the wing, the shelf — and if what is left looks the same, it is not a state. Held, set down, carried, pressed against something, standing in front of something: always the same object, no state. How the WORLD lights it is not a state — a lamp falling on it, a shadow crossing it, dusk: the scene decides that, page by page. Its OWN light is a state: a thing that glows and goes dark, lights up and goes out, changes what it gives off. Then the emission lives in the states, never in `description`, which carries only what holds on every page. A state is only when the thing itself changes — a flower wilts, a bottle breaks, a canvas gets painted, a lid is torn off, a jar is filled — or when a face prop turns its other side to us. A state's cell draws the object alone; a state defined by contact with another element cannot be drawn without that element and drags it into the cell.
- A `delta` describes the object's own look and nothing else: no place, no figure, no body part, no other element. On the first state it is how the object looks before anything happens to it; on every later state it is what changed.
- A `delta` that changes a part of the object names that part exactly as `description` names it and says what it is now: "the <part> is now <new thing>" or "the <part> is <changed condition>" (the door is now hanging from one hinge; the sail is now patched with a red cloth). It replaces that part wherever `description` names it and never adds a second one beside it. A delta that only adds a feature says so ("a bandage is now wrapped around the <part>").
- A state describes the object's OWN look — never what arrives at it from elsewhere on that page (water jetting in, a shadow falling on it, a thing thrown toward it). The arrival is the action's result and belongs with the characters in that page's prose.
- A part added to an object — a filling, an insert, a fitting, a lid, a cover — is a state of it. It earns its own entry only when BOTH hold: some page stages it on its own, away from the thing it belongs to, and it has a look worth specifying once separated.
- **A two-sided prop.** A map, letter, note, chart, book, page, sign, board or plaque is one entry with a state per side, turned away and face to camera. An object that shows a different picture on different pages — a book, an album, a board, a screen — has one face-to-camera state per distinct picture the plan lines call for. Each such state's `delta` restates what its page's plan line says the object shows, its `pages` is that page alone, and a page cites only the state whose `delta` is the picture its own plan line names. It lists the side away from the viewer first (the back of the sheet, the closed cover, the outer face of the roll), then `"face to camera"`, each with its own `pages`. Its `description` gives material, edge wear and dominant colour and says nothing about what is drawn or written on the face; words the reader must be able to read go in `text`.
- An object's `description` is drawn literally. Material, colour and shape in plain terms — never its size, which `scaleClass` alone states, the colour named with a plain colour word and a material-colour compound only where no plain word fits; never compare its SHAPE to another object ("curved like a shallow bowl") and never say who holds, carries or wears it.
- An object's `description` says what it IS and looks like, never where it is: it names no separate thing the object rests on, leans against, hangs from, lies in, is fastened to or points toward (a surface, wall, post, rail, floor, ground, shelf, person). That is page staging, and a reference cell draws the object alone. A part the object is built with (its own hook, base, handle or post) is part of it. A cell that shows the object alone is correct even when its description names a support; a cell that adds a separate support or surface fails.
- A creature's entry is written in the terms of the creature-tone block below: the ANATOMY of its face (brow, eyes, mouth, teeth, snout or beak), never a feeling or an expression, and for a creature smaller than a grown-up its body too.
A creature the story gives a powerful, wild or formidable nature is drawn as one: claws and teeth visible rather than hidden, real physical weight and presence, weathered or rugged hide, scale, fur or feather where they suit it. No rounded, toy-like or plush softening of such a creature. It may loom. A creature the story means as gentle — a pet, a domestic animal, a comic one — stays gentle and friendly-looking; the story's own nature for each creature decides which of the two it gets. Size may be whatever the story wants; a genuinely huge creature is welcome.
- As many entries as the story needs, no more. Include an element even if it appears once.
- `pages` is earned: a page belongs to an element only when that page's picture puts it in frame, never a blanket 1-19 range. Being physically present is not earning: a worn satchel, a leash on a wrist, the room they stand in are on many pages and earn only the pages that make something of them. At most 4 elements claim any one page (locations do not count); when more could, the ones the plan line names come first and the rest leave that page. An element the story leaves behind ends its range there. A character's or a tracked animal's entry claims only pages whose plan line names it. An element's `pages` always includes the page the story first brings it in — handed over, found, taken out, put on — even when that page's plan line is about something else. That is the page the reader learns what it looks like on. An element a plan line sets down at a place — put down, dropped, hidden, left behind — also claims the next two or three pages set at that same place, until a plan line moves, takes or breaks it, the story moves elsewhere, or the camera takes in the whole place from a distance; a plan line's closing "what is true after" clause is not a placement.
- Empty categories are `[]`.
- One entry per secondary character, no matter how the plan lines refer to them; a person named both by relation and by attribute is one entry. Never reuse an id. Every character the story names is declared exactly once: a name that is neither in Sarah, Saira, Facundo, Fiona, Lorena nor a `secondaryCharacters` entry is a fault, and so are two entries for the same person under different names.

Every entry needs specific colours, one signature element, and a description that works without seeing the other scenes. Which of a pair carries a one-sided feature (one limb, ear or eye that hangs, is marked or differs from its twin) is never stated as left or right and never judged by side: the specification is relational ("one hangs limp, the other is folded neatly"), and the same figure drawn with the feature on the other side matches it. A body condition the plot turns on (an injury, a hurt limb, a sign of illness) carries a visible marker a picture can show from any angle (a bandage, a splint, a sling, a plaster): the sentence that introduces the condition names the marker, the page text that first tells it names the marker, and the figure's Visual Bible description (where it has an entry) states the marker, so text and picture agree. How a limb hangs or moves is never the whole condition.

Two or more beings of one kind — two cats, two horses, a grown creature and its young — are written against each other: each entry names the dimensions they share and the dimensions that tell them apart. Unrelated ones differ in at least two a child reads at a glance: colour, markings, coat or scale texture, build, ear or horn or tail shape. Ones the story makes kin share the family look — palette, markings, eye colour, head and snout shape — and part only on age and size.
